item.title: Trapping e/4 quasiparticles in bilayer graphene
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Trapped quasiparticles in bilayer graphene show localized charge of e/4 at filling factors nu = -5/2, -1/2, and 3/2, and e/3 at nu = 2/3.

Grade 0.435 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Spins in few-electron quantum dots” · Mario Di Luca, Emily Hajigeorgiou, Ning Ma, Alexandra Waldherr, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Mitali Banerjee

Figure

Variation in transmitted resistance delta R_t plotted against antidot gate voltage V_adg and magnetic field B. Shows Coulomb-dominated conductance oscillations corresponding to minimal-excitation charges of e/4 for nu = -5/2, -1/2, 3/2 and e/3 for nu = 2/3.

Asks

Can the quasiparticle charge of even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states in bilayer graphene be measured and localized via a gate-defined antidot?

Before

Fabry–Pérot interferometers in bilayer graphene showed interferometric periodicity consistent with interfering e/2 quasiparticles enclosing e/4 localized charge.

But

Measured at B = 14 T and base temperatures below 50–70 mK; e/4 oscillations suppress rapidly above 50–70 mK.

Tools

Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene · gate-defined quantum Hall antidot · suspended air-bridge antidot gate · current-biased lock-in resistance measurements

Abstract

Measuring the charge of the quasiparticles hosted by even-denominator fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states is essential to identify the topology of their ground state. Here, we use a gate-defined antidot in bilayer graphene, with an additional gate to control only the antidot potential, to measure the charge of the quasiparticles trapped around it in even-denominator FQH states. We observe a localized charge of e/4 at ν=-5/2, -1/2, and 3/2, consistent with the minimal excitation expected for leading candidate even-denominator ground states, and e/3 at the hole-conjugate state ν=2/3. We further show that increasing the coupling between the antidot-bound states and extended edge states drives a crossover between two regimes, characterized by the minimal-excitation gate-voltage period and approximately twice that period, respectively. We discuss two possible explanations for this crossover: quasiparticle bunching and a crossover between distinct antidot transport regimes. Our results, together with previous observations of the daughter states, show that the even-denominator FQH states in bilayer graphene are compatible with a non-Abelian ground state, and that their quasiparticles can be localized around a quantum Hall antidot, a necessary ingredient for topological quantum computation.

item.title: Majorana signatures in an asymmetrically coupled quantum dot--topological superconducting nanowire junction
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Zero-temperature linear conductance for unhybridized MBSs ( u_M=0) is non-zero only at magnetic flux phase u=(2n+1) u (n∈Z) and scales as G=2qαe²/[h(α+1)]. For hybridized MBSs ( u_M≠0), conductance oscillation period shifts from 2ν to 4ν when quantum dot energy level ε_d≠ε_F.

Grade 0.409 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Spins in few-electron quantum dots” · Levente Máthé, Ioan Grosu, Liviu P. Zârbo, Ionel cTifrea

Figure

Linear conductance G mapped against magnetic flux phase φ (horizontal axis) and bias asymmetry q (vertical axis) for different leads-QD coupling ratios α. Shows conductance peak locations shifting from φ=2nπ to φ=(2n+1)π as q increases.

Asks

How do leads-QD coupling asymmetry α and bias voltage asymmetry q modify the linear conductance signatures of Majorana bound states in quantum dot-nanowire junctions?

Before

Generalizes the symmetric coupling case (α=1, q=0.5) where zero-temperature, zero-bias conductance is e²/(2h) (Liu and Baranger).

But

Theoretical calculation in the low-energy transport regime. Assumes noninteracting single-level QD and Zeeman energy E_Z>√Δ²+μ_w².

Tools

nonequilibrium Green's functions technique · p-wave topological superconductor model · Andreev reflection transport theory

Abstract

We present a theoretical study of the quantum transport through a nanoscale system in which a central quantum dot (QD) is coupled asymmetrically to normal leads and to two Majorana bound states (MBSs) localized at the ends of a topological superconducting nanowire threaded by a tunable magnetic flux. The effects of the leads--QD coupling asymmetry parameter α and the bias voltage asymmetry parameter q on the system's linear conductance are considered for the case of unhybridized and hybridized MBSs. In the zero-temperature limit, for unhybridized MBSs the system's linear conductance is finite only when the magnetic flux phase φ= (2n+1)π (n∈Z) and it scales as G=2qαe²/[h(α+1)], while for hybridized MBSs it presents a complicated dependence on the system's parameters. At finite temperature, for unhybridized MBSs, the system's linear conductance oscillates as a function of the magnetic flux phase φ with a period of 2π, and the position of the linear conductance maxima can be shifted from φ=2nπ to φ=(2n+1)π by simply varying the value of the bias voltage asymmetry parameter q. For hybridized MBSs, the conductance exhibits a similar behavior when the energy level of the central QD, ε_d, is tuned at the leads' Fermi level (ε_d=ε_F), although when ε_d≠ε_F the oscillation period changes to 4π, and the position of the linear conductance maxima depends on the actual value of ε_d and other parameters in the system. Our results highlight the experimental importance of the leads-QD and bias voltage asymmetry parameters, which are often present in realistic experimental setups, and can strongly affect the identification and observation of MBSs transport signatures.

item.title: Mobility Enhancement in Si/SiGe Quantum Well Enabled by a Buried Si Layer Trapping Oxygen Impurities
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Inserting a 6 nm buried Si trapping layer into the lower SiGe barrier cuts the oxygen background in subsequent SiGe by a factor of 5 (from ~4e17 cm^-3 to 8e16 cm^-3) and increases electron mobility.

Grade 0.406 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Spins in few-electron quantum dots” · Felix Reichmann, Alberto Mistroni, Fabian Fidorra, Giovanni Capellini, Yuji Yamamoto, Marco Lisker, Marvin H. Zoellner

Figure

Depth profile of silicon and oxygen concentrations measured by SIMS as a function of depth, showing oxygen background suppression in SiGe following an inserted 6 nm Si trapping layer.

Asks

How does oxygen reduction through heterostructure design affect transport across different carrier-density and temperature regimes in Si/SiGe quantum wells?

But

Measured on 200 mm Si(100) substrates with SiGe barriers grown at 600 °C; transport benchmarked at 1.5 K and 0.3 K on 7 devices per group.

Tools

reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RP-CVD) · secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) · Hall-bar field-effect transistors (HB-FETs) · magnetotransport

Abstract

Reducing disorder in undoped Si/SiGe field-effect heterostructures remains an important materials challenge for scalable quantum devices, particularly electron spin qubits. Background impurities such as oxygen have been identified as mobility-limiting, yet practical heterostructure-design strategies for suppressing their incorporation remain underexplored, and their influence across different transport regimes is not fully established. Here, we demonstrate a simple route to oxygen reduction and mobility enhancement in Si/SiGe quantum-well heterostructures grown by reduced-pressure chemical vapor deposition (RP-CVD) on 200 mm Si(100) substrates through the introduction of a thin, electrically passive buried Si layer within the lower SiGe barrier. Secondary-ion mass spectrometry shows that the buried Si layer reproducibly reduces the oxygen background in the subsequently grown SiGe by approximately a factor of five, without modifying the active quantum-well region. Density- and temperature-dependent magnetotransport measurements further show that this reduction increases the electron mobility, while leaving the percolation density and density-dependent mobility scaling largely unchanged. Upon cooling to 0.3 K, both high- and low-oxygen devices exhibit similar density-dependent fractional mobility enhancements, indicating that the reduced oxygen background improves momentum relaxation without substantially altering the dominant low-density disorder landscape. These results establish the buried Si layer as a straightforward and process-compatible heterostructure-design element for reducing oxygen incorporation and improving transport in 200 mm CVD-grown Si/SiGe quantum-device materials.

item.title: Distinguishing Quantum Capacitance Signatures of a Topological Majorana Wire from a Normal Wire Segment
item.description:
Worth a look new result — In a gapless normal wire, even- and odd-parity capacitance resonances are separated by 35.0 μeV in dot potential, while in a topological wire they are separated by only 5.25 μeV and persist over a gate-voltage window of -50 μeV≤δμ≤50 μeV.

Grade 0.405 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Spins in few-electron quantum dots” · Binayyak Bhusan Roy, Jay Deep Sau, Sumanta Tewari

Figure

Plots the maximum quantum capacitance over magnetic flux against dot potential detuning for gapless (left) and topological (right) wires. Gapless system shows two distinct, separated parity resonances, whereas topological system shows overlapping parity branches within a single broader gate window.

Asks

Can quantum capacitance signatures of topological Majorana zero modes be experimentally distinguished from those of a non-superconducting gapless wire segment?

But

Clean wire benchmark and correlated-disorder model with finite Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Low-energy limit involving two or three single-particle levels.

Tools

nanowire-quantum-dot interferometer model · parity-resolved quantum capacitance calculations · finite-temperature Boltzmann weighting · quasistatic charge-fluctuation averaging

Abstract

Majorana zero modes (MZMs) are spatially separated, near-zero-energy excitations expected at the ends of a topological superconducting (TS) wire. A quantum-dot interferometer can be used to probe the quantum capacitance of the TS wire, and the location and magnitude of the capacitance resonances provide information about the MZMs, while their magnetic flux dependence probes coherent coupling to the two Majorana modes. It has been recently shown that, a gapless (i.e., Δ=0) wire segment can also exhibit flux-dependent quantum capacitance oscillations through Aharonov-Bohm interference and, with suitable tuning, can reproduce a Majorana-like response. Here we show that the two mechanisms can be distinguished experimentally. In the gapless normal wire segment, the two parity-dependent signals originate from separate energy resonances corresponding to the lack of generic zero-energy states. By contrast, in the topological wire, the pair of low energy levels with even and odd parity are nearly degenerate in energy, and therefore, the two parity branches remain within the same broader resonance region in the quantum-dot potential, and persist under independent variations of the dot potential and wire chemical potential. Our results show that the experimentally observed quantum capacitance response is distinguished not by a particular flux trace at one optimized point in parameter space, but by its persistence over a finite range of independently controlled parameters, including the quantum-dot potential. This parameter space stability provides a direct means of ruling out the gapless normal wire segment as the origin of the observed Majorana-like response.

item.title: Occupation-Driven Josephson Diode in a Symmetric Junction
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Steady-state current factorizes into reciprocal spectral current and phase-asymmetric occupation imbalance I_ss=I_AP_γ, producing diode response without Andreev spectrum asymmetry.

Grade 0.403 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Coherent Manipulation of Coupled Electron Spins in Semiconductor Quantum Dots” · Jianxiong Zhai, Zelei Zhang, Jiawei Yan

Figure

Diode efficiency η_D plotted against reservoir phase χ and dissipation rate κ. Shows saturation to ideal efficiency η_D ≃1 and convergence to the analytical Zeno limit as κ increases.

Asks

Can a Josephson junction with a reciprocal Andreev channel acquire a diode response through nonequilibrium occupation?

But

Infinite-gap limit, large loss rate κ≫t,Γ, and secular limit Γ_± ≪2E_A.

Tools

double-quantum-dot junction · phase-textured nonlocal reservoir · quantum Zeno effect · Keldysh-Lindblad formalism

Abstract

We propose a Josephson diode mechanism in which nonreciprocity arises not from a conventional asymmetric Andreev spectrum but from nonequilibrium occupation of the current-carrying states engineered by attached reservoirs. We realize this mechanism in a double-quantum-dot junction, where a phase-textured nonlocal reservoir acts as a quantum Zeno selector: rapid dissipation freezes out the bright state directly coupled to the jump operator L, while preserving an orthogonal dark Andreev channel whose supercurrent remains comparable to that of the lossless junction. In the infinite-gap limit, the steady-state current factorizes as I_ss=I_A P_γ, so that even when the Andreev current I_A is strictly reciprocal, the phase asymmetry of P_γ alone can produce a Josephson diode effect through reservoir engineering. We further show that local Coulomb repulsion can drive the system toward a nearly ideal diode regime via a dark-pair resonance. Using Keldysh-Lindblad calculations, we demonstrate that our results remain robust for realistic junctions with a finite superconducting gap and dissipation.

item.title: Topologically protected perfect crossed Andreev reflection in flux-engineered quantum wire junctions
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Crossed Andreev reflection achieves 100% probability (P_CAR=1) at flux φ=π. Nonlocal differential conductance reaches G_RL=-2e²/h.

Grade 0.401 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “double quantum dot exchange gates” · Abhiram Soori

Figure

Logarithmic nonlocal conductance η mapped against interface energy ε₀ and junction hopping t'/t. The closed loop yields a topological phase winding number W=1, protecting a zero-reflection node (unit CAR).

Asks

Can crossed Andreev reflection be isolated with 100% efficiency without using exotic topological materials?

But

Requires magnetic flux φ=π, tuned junction hopping t' ≃t/√2, and bias within superconducting gap |eV| < Δ. Holds under weak bond and onsite disorder.

Tools

tight-binding BdG model · scattering matrix theory · Cauchy argument principle · cross-correlation shot noise

Abstract

Generating non-locally entangled electron pairs via Cooper-pair splitting is vital for solid-state quantum information processing. However, isolating the underlying crossed Andreev reflection (CAR) is challenging due to competing transport processes like electron tunneling (ET) and local Andreev reflection (AR). Here, we propose a flux-tunable four-terminal normal metal-superconductor junction that achieves deterministic, 100% efficient CAR. We demonstrate that at exactly half a magnetic flux quantum (φ=π), exact destructive Aharonov-Bohm and Peierls interferences structurally forbid ET and AR respectively. By tuning the central junction hopping, electron reflection is also suppressed to zero. Using the Cauchy argument principle, we prove that this suppression manifests as a quantized topological winding number, guaranteeing a topologically protected unit CAR probability. We establish that this regime is characterized by a strictly positive cross-correlation shot noise, providing an unambiguous experimental signature of Cooper-pair splitting. Furthermore, this perfect CAR is nearly broadband within the superconducting gap and remarkably robust against structural disorder, offering a highly resilient architecture for deterministic nonlocal entanglement generation.
